headline: Island Treaties, AI Songs and Sharks Without Fins
teaser: Can a small nation stay safe without losing its freedom? Should music apps delete songs made by machines? And is half a rule better than none for the ocean's sharks?

articles.title: A New Security Partner: Solomon Islands Turns to Australia
articles.dek: A small Pacific nation has chosen Australia as its main security partner. Has it gained a reliable friend, or swapped one kind of dependence for another?
paras: On Wednesday, in a ceremony at Parliament House in Canberra, the prime ministers of Australia and Solomon Islands signed a treaty that both men described as historic. Under the agreement, Solomon Islands names Australia as its “primary security partner” and promises that no foreign military or security base will be built on its territory. The country of fewer than 900,000 people, spread across hundreds of islands about 2,000 kilometres northeast of Australia, rarely makes world headlines. This week, however, it found itself at the centre of a quiet but intense competition for influence in the Pacific.

To understand why the treaty matters, it helps to go back to 2022. That year, the government of then-prime minister Manasseh Sogavare signed a security pact with China that allowed Chinese police training teams to work in the country. Today, roughly two dozen Chinese officers are present at any one time. The deal alarmed Canberra and Washington, which feared it could one day open the door to a Chinese naval presence close to Australia's shores. Australia's foreign minister, Penny Wong, has called the pact the country's worst foreign policy blunder in the Pacific since the Second World War.

The new treaty attempts to reverse that situation. Beyond the ban on foreign bases, Solomon Islands commits to keeping its sensitive infrastructure free from militarisation and foreign interference, and it agrees to consult Australia on matters of national security. It also accepts that security assistance should come first from members of the Pacific Islands Forum, the region's main political body, with outside partners called in only for needs those members cannot meet. In return, Australia has pledged a package that the ABC reports is worth about A$740 million, most of it in grants, to support free education, infrastructure, the national budget and the police. Australia will also open new work pathways in sectors such as aged care and childcare.

Notably, the treaty does not explicitly forbid cooperation with China, and Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who took office in May, has been careful with his words. Media reports say his government has told Beijing that the 2022 pact will not be renewed when its five-year term ends in 2027, but Wale declined to confirm this, pointing to a confidentiality clause in the agreement. China's foreign ministry responded that its cooperation with Pacific nations is not aimed at any third party and involves no geopolitical rivalry.

Supporters see the treaty as a sensible choice for a small nation. Australia is the closest large neighbour and the biggest aid donor in the region, and, in their view, a more predictable partner. Wale himself suggested that under the previous government his country had become a source of uncertainty and doubt for its neighbours, and that the treaty helps restore trust. Oliver Nobetau of the Lowy Institute, an Australian think tank, called the deal a “massive win” for Canberra, which has already signed similar agreements with Fiji, Tuvalu, Vanuatu and Papua New Guinea.

Critics, however, see a different picture. Sogavare, now leader of the opposition, warned that abandoning the China pact could damage valuable development ties with Beijing and accused Wale of “dancing to Australia's tune.” Some opposition figures describe the money flowing to constituency funds controlled by members of parliament as “chequebook diplomacy,” suggesting that loyalty is being bought rather than earned. Even observers who welcome the treaty raise questions: Nobetau asked what exactly Australia had offered in exchange, and others argue that Australia's reputation will depend on whether the promised money and support are actually delivered.

The deeper question is whether small states can benefit from great-power competition without becoming its victims. For years, Pacific leaders have argued that their most urgent security threat is not a foreign army but climate change, rising seas and fragile economies. A treaty that brings schools, jobs and police training may serve those goals, even if its main purpose in Canberra is strategic. Yet when a country promises to consult one partner on its security choices, it also gives up a degree of freedom. Whether Solomon Islands has gained a reliable friend or simply exchanged one form of dependence for another may only become clear years from now.

write.p:
Dr. Patel: This week, Solomon Islands signed a treaty naming Australia as its main security partner, in exchange for about A$740 million in support. Some people think small countries should choose one strong partner for safety. Others believe they should stay neutral and work with every power. Which approach do you think is better for a small nation, and why?
Mia: “I think choosing one partner is wiser. A clear partnership brings real money for schools and police, and neighbours know where the country stands. Trying to please everyone often means no one fully trusts you.”
Leo: “I disagree. If a small nation depends on one partner, it loses bargaining power. Staying neutral lets it accept help from many sides and keep control over its own decisions.”
steps: State your position clearly in the first sentence.
Respond to Mia or Leo and add a new reason.
Support it with a fact from the article (A$740 million, no foreign bases, the 2022 China pact).

articles.title: Drowning in “AI Slop”: A Music App Decides to Delete Millions of Songs
articles.dek: One streaming service is removing songs made entirely by AI. Is a ban the best way to protect human musicians, or will it be impossible to draw the line?
paras: Imagine opening a music app and discovering that almost half of the newest songs were not written, played or sung by any human being. According to the streaming service TIDAL, that is roughly the situation it now faces. On Tuesday, the company announced that, starting on 9 December, it will begin removing music made entirely by artificial intelligence from its catalogue and will refuse to accept any more of it. Songs that musicians create with the help of AI tools will still be welcome; only tracks that are 100 percent machine-made will be banned.

The numbers behind the decision are striking. TIDAL says that more than 43 percent of the tracks uploaded to the service over the past 90 days were identified as fully AI-generated. In total, about 27 million such tracks, or 6.3 percent of its entire catalogue, now sit on the platform, and roughly 96 percent of them have never been streamed even once. Critics have a name for this flood of cheap, mass-produced content: “AI slop.” Because modern AI tools can produce a complete song in seconds, a single uploader can release thousands of tracks, hoping that a few will earn small payments or slip into automated playlists.

TIDAL's new rule is a sharp escalation of its earlier approach. In June, the company stopped paying royalties for fully AI-generated tracks and began marking them with an “AI” label, a policy that took effect in July. Yet the uploads kept coming. Robert Anderson, who leads TIDAL's music team, said the earlier step had not been enough and that “something more drastic needs to be done.” Under the new system, distributors, the companies that deliver music to streaming services, will no longer be allowed to send fully AI-made songs, and any submission whose information shows it was created entirely by AI will be rejected.

Supporters argue that the ban protects both listeners and human artists. When millions of near-identical tracks crowd a catalogue, they say, genuine music becomes harder to discover, and new musicians, who already struggle for attention, are pushed even further out of sight. TIDAL itself acknowledged that not every song catches on immediately and that artists need time to build an audience; the problem, it argued, is that at this scale authentic work is simply buried. From this perspective, a clear rule is fairer than an endless contest between spammers and detection software.

Other companies, however, have chosen different paths, which shows that the right response is far from obvious. Bandcamp, a platform popular with independent musicians, banned AI-generated music outright in January. Spotify and YouTube Music, by contrast, have preferred to label AI music rather than remove it, leaving listeners to decide what they want to hear. Meanwhile, the music industry is also exploring AI as a business opportunity: an estimate by the investment bank Goldman Sachs suggests that licensing music for AI could increase record-label revenue by about 10 percent by 2035.

The ban also raises difficult practical questions. Where exactly is the line between a song that is assisted by AI and one that is generated by it? A producer might use AI to suggest a melody, clean up a recording or create a backing track; at what point does the human contribution become too small to count? Detection tools can make mistakes, and labels that depend on uploaders honestly describing their own work can be gamed. A system that is too strict risks punishing real artists, while one that is too loose may change very little.

In the end, TIDAL's decision is less about technology than about values. It asks what a music platform is for: a neutral warehouse that stores anything anyone uploads, or a curated space that promises listeners human creativity. As AI tools improve, every streaming service will have to answer that question, and the answers they choose may shape not only what we hear but also whether making music remains a realistic career for the next generation of artists.

articles.title: Fins Attached? A Hard-Won Compromise to Protect Atlantic Sharks
articles.dek: After 18 failed attempts, Atlantic nations have agreed on new shark finning rules. Is a partial step real progress, or just a new way to delay a stronger ban?
paras: For more than two decades, cutting the fins off sharks and throwing the rest of the animal back into the sea has been banned in the Atlantic Ocean, at least on paper. Enforcing that ban, however, has proved remarkably difficult. This week, at the end of the annual meeting of the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) in Vilamoura, Portugal, governments finally agreed on stronger rules. Many delegations welcomed the result, and the European Union described it as a landmark. Yet several conservation groups say the deal is full of loopholes, and that a better option was blocked.

Shark finning exists because of a simple economic imbalance. Shark fins, used mainly in soup, sell for far more than shark meat, so some fishers have an incentive to keep only the fins and discard the bodies, which take up valuable space on board. The practice is wasteful and cruel, but it also creates a scientific problem. Once a shark's body is gone, inspectors at the port often cannot tell which species the fins came from, making it much easier to hide catches of protected sharks or to exceed fishing limits.

Conservationists have long argued that the simplest solution is a rule requiring all sharks to be landed with their fins “naturally attached.” If the fins stay on the body, the animal can be identified, and fishers gain little by throwing carcasses overboard. Such a proposal had been put forward at ICCAT 18 times before and had never passed, largely because of opposition from Japan, whose fleets argue that keeping the fins attached is impractical for sharks that are frozen at sea during long voyages.

The compromise adopted this year reflects that disagreement. Sharks landed fresh must now keep their fins naturally attached. For frozen sharks, however, countries may use alternative methods, including a Japanese-led option that allows fins to be tied to the body, or removed, tagged and stored in the same hold as the rest of the shark. Other methods involve wires, ropes or tags. Under certain conditions, the rules could lead to a full fins-attached requirement around 2029 or 2030, but critics point out that the alternatives might remain in use for years.

Reactions were sharply divided. Supporters argue that, after so many failed attempts, a partial step is better than none, and that the agreement proves that progress is still possible in a body that usually makes decisions by consensus. Conservation groups were far less enthusiastic. Nicolas Blanc of the Portuguese group Sciaena said campaigners were “not going to be opening the champagne bottle” until a rule without exceptions is in place. Sonja Fordham of Shark Advocates International warned that the alternatives are overly complicated, largely untested and could even add more debris to the ocean.

The meeting produced other mixed results. Delegates kept in place a ban on retaining North Atlantic shortfin mako sharks, a fast-swimming species whose numbers have fallen sharply, and rejected a United States proposal to reopen a limited mako fishery. Ali Hood of the Shark Trust welcomed that decision but urged countries to reduce the bycatch of blue sharks, which are often caught by accident on lines set for tuna and swordfish. ICCAT also agreed to look more closely at whether members follow existing rules, after most of them had reported poor data on sharks and, between 2016 and 2024, most had reported no discards at all.

The story of the Atlantic shark rules illustrates a familiar dilemma in international environmental law. Strict rules are easier to enforce but harder to agree on, while flexible rules win broad support but may change little on the water. Sharks, which grow slowly and produce few young, cannot recover quickly from overfishing, so delays have real costs. Whether this year's compromise becomes a stepping stone toward a stronger ban or simply a new way to postpone one will depend on how seriously member countries apply it in the years ahead.

parts.title: Multiple-choice cloze
parts.task: Read the text and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap.
parts.text: Solomon Islands rarely {1} the headlines, but this week it signed a treaty that could reshape its foreign relations. Under the agreement, Australia becomes the country's main security partner, and no foreign base may be built on its soil. Supporters say the deal will {2} an end to years of uncertainty. Critics, however, fear the government has {3} in to pressure from Canberra. The prime minister has refused to {4} light on whether the 2022 pact with China will be renewed, saying he is bound by a confidentiality clause. Either way, Australia's support package is {5} to boost spending on schools and the police. Analysts say the real test will be whether Australia {6} up to its promises. For a nation of fewer than a million people, staying on good {7} with powerful neighbours is a delicate balancing {8}.

items.why: We say a person or event “makes the headlines.” The other verbs do not form this collocation.
“Put an end to” means to stop something completely. “Make”, “give” and “draw” do not form this fixed phrase.
“Give in to” means to stop resisting and accept what someone wants. “Fall in”, “hand in” and “turn in” have different meanings.
“Shed light on” means to make something clearer or easier to understand. The other verbs do not combine with “light on” in this meaning.
“Be expected to do” is a common passive pattern. We cannot say “is hoped/wished/awaited to boost.”
“Live up to promises/expectations” means to do what was promised. The other verbs do not form this phrase with “up to”.
“On good terms with” means having a friendly relationship. “Relations” and “ties” are not used with “on good … with”.
“A balancing act” is a fixed expression for trying to satisfy several competing demands at once.

parts.title: Open cloze
parts.task: Read the text and think of the word which best fits each gap. Use only one word in each gap.
parts.text: Streaming service TIDAL has announced that it will remove songs made entirely by artificial intelligence. {9} to the company, more than 43 percent of recent uploads were fully AI-generated, and most of {10} have never been played. Songs created with the help of AI tools, {11} the other hand, will still be accepted. The decision follows an earlier policy {12} which TIDAL stopped paying royalties for such tracks. {13} the earlier step had little effect, the company decided that stronger action was needed. Critics point out that it is not always easy to tell {14} a song was made by a person or a machine. Others argue that platforms should label AI music rather {15} delete it. Whatever happens, the debate is unlikely to go away any time {16}.

items.why: “According to the company” introduces the source of information.
“Most of them” refers back to the uploads. After “of” we need an object pronoun.
“On the other hand” introduces a contrasting point.
“A policy under which…” (or “in which”) uses a preposition before the relative pronoun “which”.
The clause gives the reason for stronger action, so a reason linker such as “because”, “since” or “as” is needed.
“Tell whether/if…” introduces an indirect yes/no question about two possibilities.
“Rather than” means “instead of”.
“Any time soon” is used in negative contexts to mean “in the near future”.

parts.title: Word formation
parts.task: Use the word given in capitals to form a word that fits in the gap.
parts.text: For years, the ban on shark finning in the Atlantic existed mainly on paper, because {17} was so difficult. Fins are far more {18} than shark meat, so some fishers discarded the bodies at sea. Without the body, it is almost {19} to identify the species. This week, governments reached a {20} agreement: fresh sharks must keep their fins attached, while frozen sharks may use other methods. Conservation groups described the exceptions as {21} complicated and warned that they had not been properly tested. Supporters, however, praised the {22} of nations that had disagreed for decades. Because sharks grow slowly, any delay in {23} could have serious consequences, and scientists will be watching closely to see whether the new rules are applied {24}.

items.why: After “because” we need a noun subject: enforce → enforcement.
“far more … than” needs an adjective: value → valuable.
The meaning is negative (“almost … to identify”), so add the prefix im-: impossible.
“Historic” means important in history; “historical” means connected with the past, which does not fit an agreement just made.
An adverb is needed before the adjective “complicated”, with a negative meaning: unnecessarily.
After “praised the” we need a noun: willing → willingness.
After the preposition “in” we need a noun: protect → protection.
The gap describes how the rules are applied, so an adverb is needed: effectively.
